contentBlocks.text: This week you've learned four separate exponent rules. Today: combine them all in one problem!

Real algebra problems often need more than one exponent rule at once. Simplify (x³)² · x⁻¹ step by step: first apply the power-of-a-power rule to (x³)², giving x⁶, then apply the product rule to x⁶ · x⁻¹, giving x⁵ (since 6+(-1)=5). Simplify (y²)⁴ · y⁻³ using the same two-step approach.
You just combined multiple exponent rules in one problem! Tomorrow we'll review everything from this week.

objectives: Apply the power-of-a-power rule and the product rule together in one multi-step problem
Correctly simplify (y²)⁴ · y⁻³ using both rules in sequence
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's four rules together.
2. Model the (x³)²·x⁻¹ example step by step.
3. Have the child simplify (y²)⁴·y⁻³ independently.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's cumulative review.
differentiationTips: Struggling: have the child write out each step separately on paper rather than trying to combine rules mentally
Ready for more: ask the child to create their own two-rule combined problem for a family member to solve
This is the week's synthesis moment — combining rules in sequence, one step at a time, is the genuinely important skill here
teacherGuide.answerKey: (y²)⁴ = y⁸ (2×4=8), then y⁸·y⁻³ = y⁵ (8+(-3)=5). So (y²)⁴·y⁻³ = y⁵.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Algebra 1 standards on properties of exponents, synthesizing this week's four rules into one coherent problem-solving skill before tomorrow's review.

generationData.instructions: Simplify each expression using more than one exponent rule.
